Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i'm looking for cello lessons for my daughter, Maya, and possibly for myself too, and I wondered if you might be able to tell me what kind of arrangement could work. Maya is thirteen and has played violin at school for about a year and a half, but she has never had a private teacher or played cello. I took piano lessons as a child and remember how to read music slowly, though I haven't practiced regularly for years. We are interested in cello for different reasons, so I don't know whether it would make sense for us to study with one teacher or whether that would make scheduling more complicated.

Maya has been asking about cello since she heard the low part in her school orchestra concert in November. She likes the sound of the instrument and wants to learn how the bow makes a note change from warm and quiet to a little sharper. She told me, “I want to learn the theme from Spirited Away, but I don't want every lesson to be movie music.” I thought that was a useful way of explaining what she likes: she has a few pieces in mind, but she also wants to learn the basics and play music that isn't from films. She reads treble clef from violin, but bass clef and the different finger spacing would both be new for her.

For me, I am mostly interested in playing folk and older dance tunes, rather than preparing for an exam or joining an orchestra. I have a folder with about twenty tunes in it, including “The Ash Grove” and “Morrison's Jig,” but I know I would need to learn proper bowing and fingering before trying to play them at a sensible speed. I have not settled on a cello yet. My neighbor has offered to lend me a full-size instrument for a few weeks, but we haven't checked its condition, and I don't know whether the bridge and strings are suitable. Maya might need a smaller size; she is about five feet tall, and I don't know if a 3/4 cello would fit her or if that should be decided in person.

Could you let me know whether you teach beginners around Maya's age, and whether you take on adults who are starting again after a long break? If you do teach both, I'd be glad to hear whether you think it is practical for us to have separate lessons with you, perhaps one after the other, or if it would be better for Maya to start on her own. I am not asking for a joint lesson necessarily, since our goals and experience are different. I would just like to understand the options before we try to arrange instruments and travel.

We are usually free on Tuesdays after 4:30 and on Saturday mornings before 11:30. Thursdays can sometimes work, but Maya has orchestra rehearsal on two Thursdays each month, and the date changes according to the school calendar. We could probably manage a 30- or 45-minute lesson, depending on what you recommend for a beginner. If lessons for the two of us were close together, I could wait nearby while Maya has hers. We live near the east end of Alder Street, so the studio on Pine Road would be easiest for us to reach. We could also consider an online lesson for me if that is something you offer, although Maya would need in-person help with posture and the bow at the beginning.

A few practical questions would help us figure out what to do next:
1. Do students need to own or rent a cello before the first lesson, or is there an instrument available to try during an introductory meeting? If we rent one, could you suggest a shop that lets us change sizes if Maya grows into a different instrument?
2. Do you offer a short first lesson or trial meeting, and what is the current fee for a regular 30- or 45-minute lesson? We would also like to know whether payment is by the lesson or in monthly blocks, and how much notice you need if we have to cancel because of a school event or illness.
3. Do you usually provide books or a list of music to buy, or should a beginner wait until after the first lesson? Maya has a music stand and a violin shoulder rest, but no cello supplies. I have a tuner and a music folder, though my tuner is several years old and I don't know if it can pick up the cello's lower strings reliably.

At home, there is room to practice in the living room, but it is not completely quiet. My partner works from home on Wednesdays and takes calls until about 5:00, so that is not a good regular practice time. We could probably set aside twenty minutes on most evenings, and a little longer on Sundays, but we do not want to promise daily practice before we know what a realistic beginner routine looks like. Maya has orchestra on Mondays, and I would like to avoid making every evening feel like another scheduled class. It would be helpful if you could tell us what you normally expect between lessons, especially in the first few months.

We would also appreciate knowing how you handle repertoire and progress. Maya is happy to work on scales and exercises if she understands what they are helping her do, and I would like a mix of reading music and learning tunes by ear. Neither of us needs a formal performance, but Maya's school has a small spring concert in May, and she may want to take part if she is ready. That is not a requirement for starting lessons, and I wouldn't want to assume she could prepare a piece by then. Please let us know if you have a usual approach to setting goals with new students, or if that is something you talk through after you meet them.

If you need more information about Maya's violin experience, my previous piano lessons, our possible instrument situation, or the days we can travel, I can send it along. For now, an idea of your beginner lesson options, fees, and instrument recommendations would help us decide what to ask about next. Autumn instrument lessons at the Riverside Arts Room

registration for the fall set of instrument lessons at Riverside Arts Room is opening on September 3. The first lessons start the week of October 7, and the last regular lessons are the week of December 9. This is a ten week session, not including the Thanksgiving closure, and it is for people who want to begin an instrument or continue from an earlier class. The building is at 18 Mill Street, in the second floor rooms above the library. The entrance is the side door facing the small parking lot, not the door on Mill Street itself. There is no elevator in this building, which people should know before they register.

The lessons being offered are piano, guitar, violin, and hand percussion. Piano and guitar have both individual lessons and small group lessons; violin is individual only this session, and hand percussion is group only. The individual lesson is 30 minutes each week. Group lessons are 45 minutes each week, with four students as the maximum in a group. The groups will be formed according to the students' experience, not by a placement test. Beginners are welcome, and people do not need to read music before starting. The program is for students aged eight and older. A student younger than twelve must have an adult remain in the building during the lesson, although the adult does not need to sit in the classroom.

1. The weekly schedule is not identical for every instrument. Piano lessons take place on Tuesdays between 3:30 and 7:00 p.m.; guitar lessons take place on Wednesdays between 4:00 and 7:30 p.m.; violin lessons take place on Thursdays between 3:30 and 6:30 p.m.; and hand percussion meets on Saturdays from 10:00 a.m. to 12:15 p.m. The exact time inside a listed window is set after registration, and the office will contact people about it by September 24. A requested time can be noted on the form, but it is not guaranteed. There are no lessons during the closure from November 27 through November 29. Saturday hand percussion is not affected by that closure.

There are two instructors this fall. Mara Ellis teaches piano and has taught at the room for six years. Daniel Cho teaches guitar and violin; he is returning after teaching the spring session. Hand percussion is taught by Asha Bell, who also coordinates the program. Bell said, “We want the first lesson to feel manageable, whether someone is learning their first notes or finding their way back to an instrument.” The instructors provide a weekly practice sheet, but students are not required to practice a particular number of minutes. Families can ask instructors about a practice plan after the first lesson.

2. The ten-week session fees are $240 for an individual lesson and $125 for a group lesson. Payment is due when the place is confirmed, rather than with the first lesson. The room accepts card, check, or cash, and a payment plan can be requested by email before registration is complete. The group price is per student, not per family. There is no separate registration fee. If a student withdraws after the second lesson, the remaining unused lesson fees can be refunded; there is no refund for lessons already held. The room does not yet know whether there will be a winter session.

Students may bring their own instrument. The Arts Room has four practice keyboards, three full-size guitars, two violins, and a set of hand percussion instruments that students can use during lessons. These instruments stay at the room and cannot be taken home. Guitar students should bring a pick if they have one, but a pick is not required for the first lesson. Violin students need a shoulder rest only if their instructor recommends one after the first meeting. Piano students do not need to bring books. For students who need an instrument at home, the office can share contact details for two local music shops that offer rentals; it does not rent instruments itself.

3. Registration can be made through the form on the Riverside Arts Room website or on paper at the library information desk. The form asks for the student's name, age, chosen instrument, whether they prefer an individual or group lesson where both are offered, previous experience, and two possible time windows. It also asks for an emergency contact and a phone number that can receive day-of schedule messages. A parent or guardian must complete the form for a student under eighteen. The form does not require payment information. Registration remains open until September 20, unless a class fills earlier. There are six individual spaces for each instrument and eight spaces in each group lesson. If a group is full, the office can put a student on a waiting list, but a place is not assured.

There is no audition, and registration does not guarantee a particular instructor or requested time. The office will email a confirmation or a waiting-list notice by September 24. Anyone who has a question about choosing a class can email lessons@riversidearts.example or leave a message at 555-0146. The office returns calls on Mondays and Thursdays. People who need information about the building entrance or the stairs can ask before registering. The second-floor rooms are reached by one flight of stairs, and there is no lift.

4. A short student sharing time is being considered for December 14 at 11:00 a.m. It has not been confirmed, and participation would be optional if it takes place. The instructors will ask students later in the session whether they would like to play something for families and other students. No student needs to perform to complete the lessons, and the sharing time is not included in the session fee. More information will be sent if the room and date are confirmed.

The announcement and registration form are available at the library information desk during its regular hours. The desk can provide paper forms, but it cannot answer questions about lesson times or payments; those questions should go to the Arts Room office. The September 3 opening date applies to both online and paper registration.
